clinicalPearls: A perforating dermatosis defined by transepidermal elimination of abnormal elastic fibres, presenting as keratotic papules arranged in serpiginous or arcuate (annular) configurations.
Typically affects adolescents and young adults, with a male predominance, and favours the sides of the neck, the face, upper limbs and flexures.

Idiopathic in many cases, but classically associated with inherited connective-tissue and metabolic disorders: Down syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, pseudoxanthoma elasticum, Marfan syndrome and osteogenesis imperfecta.
A distinctive drug-induced form is caused by penicillamine, which produces bizarre 'lumpy-bumpy' or 'bramble-bush' abnormal elastic fibres on staining.

Histology shows increased and abnormal elastic fibres in the papillary dermis being extruded through a channel in the hyperplastic epidermis; elastic tissue stains (Verhoeff-van Gieson) are diagnostic.
Lesions are often asymptomatic or mildly pruritic and may resolve spontaneously over months to years, sometimes leaving atrophic or reticulate scarring.

Treatment is challenging and often unsatisfactory; options include topical retinoids or corticosteroids, cryotherapy, and laser or cautery for limited disease, with withdrawal of penicillamine in drug-induced cases.
The serpiginous configuration reflects centrifugal spread with central clearing rather than a single perforating focus.
reference.pathophysiology: Elastosis perforans serpiginosa results from focal accumulation of qualitatively and quantitatively abnormal elastic fibres in the papillary dermis, which the skin eliminates transepidermally as a foreign-body-type response. The epidermis surrounding a follicular or interfollicular channel becomes hyperplastic and forms a narrow perforating canal through which the altered elastic material, admixed with keratinous and inflammatory debris, is expelled. In heritable connective-tissue disorders the elastic fibres are intrinsically abnormal, while penicillamine directly interferes with elastin cross-linking (by inhibiting lysyl oxidase-dependent desmosine formation), producing the characteristic serrated 'thorny' elastic fibres seen on histology.
additionalInvestigations: skin biopsy with elastic tissue stain (Verhoeff-van Gieson) to demonstrate abnormal elastic fibres and their transepidermal elimination
medication history focused on penicillamine and duration of use
clinical and, where indicated, genetic assessment for associated connective-tissue disorders
karyotype or clinical evaluation for Down syndrome when phenotypic features present
ophthalmic and cardiovascular review if pseudoxanthoma elasticum or Marfan syndrome is suspected
dermoscopy to highlight keratotic plugs in an annular arrangement
redFlags: current or prior penicillamine therapy indicating a drug-induced form requiring drug review
features of an underlying heritable connective-tissue disorder with systemic (ocular, cardiovascular, skeletal) implications
extensive or rapidly spreading serpiginous plaques causing significant scarring
secondary infection of excoriated or treated lesions
reference.prognosis: Often a self-limiting condition that resolves over months to a few years, though it may leave atrophic or reticulate scarring; drug-induced and syndrome-associated forms can be more persistent and recurrence after destructive treatment is common.
pitfalls: omitting an elastic tissue stain, so the diagnostic abnormal elastic fibres are missed on routine sections
failing to elicit a penicillamine history in a young patient with connective-tissue disease
mistaking annular lesions for tinea corporis or granuloma annulare and treating empirically
aggressive destructive therapy leading to disfiguring scarring given the tendency to spontaneous resolution
management: Withdrawal of causative penicillamine in the drug-induced form as the key disease-modifying step
Reassurance and observation, since many idiopathic cases resolve spontaneously over months to years
Topical therapy for symptomatic or persistent lesions using topical retinoids, topical corticosteroids and emollients
Physical or destructive treatments in selected cases such as cryotherapy, curettage or laser, weighed against a high recurrence rate and risk of scarring
Antipruritic measures where lesions are itchy
Evaluation and management of associated conditions including Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, pseudoxanthoma elasticum, Marfan syndrome, osteogenesis imperfecta and Down syndrome
Dermatology referral for diagnostic confirmation by skin biopsy with elastic-tissue stains and treatment planning
